cards.back: About 20M new reviews a day, 1.8B to backfill, about 40 languages and 15 categories. Today's keyword rules agree with human raters about 60% of the time.

cards.front: Cost of an LLM per review
cards.back: At about 400 tokens in and 10 out, roughly $2,900 a day, or about $87K a month. That is the expensive default, not the design.
An LLM labels about 50K reviews once, experts check a sample, and a small multilingual classifier is trained on them.
Low top probability (below about 0.7), a close top two, or a high-stakes class like payments sends the review to the LLM. Still unsure goes to raters, whose labels feed training.
Classifier GPU plus about 10% of reviews at LLM prices comes to about $10K a month instead of $87K.
Raising it makes auto-tags more precise but sends more reviews to the LLM. Illustratively 0.7 gives about 10% to the LLM and 93% precision; 0.9 gives about 30% and $27K a month.
Two raters on an overlap set with Cohen's kappa of 0.7 or more, an adjudicator for disagreements, and 200 or more examples per key class.
With about 40 examples a measured 90% recall is uncertain by roughly ±9 points; with 400 it is about ±3.
Per-class precision and recall with recall of 90% or more on crash and payments, macro-F1 of 0.85 or more, and no top-10 language more than 5 points below average.

cards.front: Who counts in the weekly summary
cards.back: SQL computes counts and spikes over the tags; the LLM only writes text from those results, and code checks every number.
Randomised by developer, primary metric is the share of reviews replied to within 7 days, with rating change and complaints as guardrails, run for at least 2 full weeks.

quiz.q: The classifier reports 94% accuracy but developers say payments issues are missing from the summary. What do you check first?
choices: Overall accuracy on a bigger test set
Per-class recall on payments and the confusion matrix
The LLM judge's agreement score
Average review length
quiz.why: Accuracy hides rare classes, so per-class precision and recall show whether payments is being missed.

quiz.q: Finance says the LLM bill tripled. The share of reviews sent to the LLM went from 10% to 30%. Which knob most likely moved?
choices: The confidence threshold was raised, toward 0.9
The kappa target was lowered
The A/B test was extended
The SQL spike rule changed
quiz.why: A higher threshold sends more reviews to the LLM; illustratively 0.9 means about 30% and $27K a month.

quiz.q: Crash tags jump 6× overnight, but most new reviews are near-identical one-liners. What should the weekly job do before reporting a spike?
choices: Ask the LLM whether it looks real
Raise the classifier threshold
Dedupe near-duplicate and bot reviews before counting
Report it; counts are counts
quiz.why: Review bombing should not look like a real spike, so dedupe comes before counting.

quiz.q: A teammate proposes an LLM judge to grade the classifier's tags on the golden set. What is the right response?
choices: Yes, calibrate the judge on 100 human labels
Use two judges and average them
Use the keyword rules as the judge
Not needed: compare predicted and gold labels in code
quiz.why: Every golden item already has a gold label, so a judge adds nothing for classification.

quiz.q: The drafts A/B test shows reply rate up with p < 0.05, but ratings after a reply fell. What do you do?
choices: Block the launch: the guardrail failed, so drafts make replies more frequent but worse
Ship it, the primary metric is significant
Rerun it randomised by review
Drop the rating guardrail
quiz.why: A guardrail failure blocks launch even when the primary lift is significant.

quiz.q: Precision on payments drops on the fresh weekly labelled sample after a new payment method launches, while the input language mix is unchanged. What is this?
choices: Data drift
Concept drift: the meaning of the tag shifted
Label leakage
A sample-size problem
quiz.why: Concept drift is detected by precision and recall falling on fresh labels; data drift is a change in input distributions.

quiz.q: Why not use the existing keyword rules as the first stage to decide which reviews are easy?
choices: Keywords are too slow at 20M a day
Keywords cannot handle 40 languages at all
They fire on almost every review and are confidently wrong about 40% of the time, so they cannot judge easiness
Keyword rules cost more than the LLM
quiz.why: The classifier's own confidence can decide which reviews are easy; keywords cannot.
